meta.title: Who really said "They that love beyond the World, cannot be separated by it. Death cannot kill, what never dies"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuinely William Penn — maxims 127 and 128 of "Union of Friends" in More Fruits of Solitude, London 1718. Verified in the scanned first edition.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'They that love beyond the World, cannot be separated by it. Death cannot kill, what never dies'?
meta.ogDescription: Penn wrote it as two numbered maxims, not one sentence. Confirmed in the 1718 first edition of More Fruits of Solitude.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1644–1718 · English Quaker writer, founder of Pennsylvania
answer.sourceLine: Genuine, and traceable to the page. Both sentences appear in More Fruits of Solitude, the second part of Penn’s Reflections and Maxims, under the heading “Union of Friends” — but Penn printed them as two separately numbered maxims, 127 and 128, not as the single sentence that circulates today. Confirmed in the 1718 London edition scanned by the Internet Archive ↗.

source.heading: The maxims, as Penn printed them

docMeta.dd: More Fruits of Solitude: Being the Second Part of Reflections and Maxims, Relating to the Conduct of Human Life
London: Printed and Sold by the Assigns of J. Sowle, at the Bible in George-Yard, Lombard-Street, 1718
William Penn (1644–1718), published anonymously in his lifetime

source.excerpt:
127. They that love beyond the World, cannot be separated by it.
128. Death cannot kill, what never dies.
129. Nor can Spirits ever be divided that love and live in the same Divine Principle; the Root and Record of their Friendship.
130. If Absence be not Death, neither is theirs.
131. Death is but Crossing the World, as Friends do the Seas; They live in one another still.
trail: Searched the scanned 1718 London edition of More Fruits of Solitude ↗ and found both sentences under the running head “Union of Friends,” numbered 127 and 128, with the imprint “Printed and Sold by the Assigns of J. Sowle, at the Bible in George-Yard, Lombard-Street.”

Cross-checked the clean text of the 1903 H. M. Caldwell reprint ↗, whose introduction by Edmund Gosse states that the first part was licensed on 24 May 1693, that More Fruits made its earliest appearance in 1718, and that this reprint follows the 1718 text rather than the 1693 one.

Confirmed the maxim numbers against Wikiquote’s sourced William Penn page ↗, which carries the passage cited to numbers 127–134 of Part II. Quote Investigator has no entry on this line — there is no attribution dispute to settle, only a wording one.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the “Union of Friends” section. Penn numbered each sentence separately; the quotation everyone knows is 127 and 128 run together. The section continues to 134.

source.rightsNote: More Fruits of Solitude was printed in London in 1718 and has been reprinted continuously since; the text is long out of copyright in the United States, as any work first published before 1931 is. The wording quoted here is Penn’s own English, not a translation, so no separate translator’s copyright attaches. The Internet Archive’s 1903 reprint is likewise flagged NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT.

author.name: William Penn
author.heading: About William Penn
author.metaLine: 1644–1718 · English Quaker writer and founder of Pennsylvania
author.bio: William Penn was an English Quaker who was jailed repeatedly for his beliefs — including a stretch in the Tower of London in 1668–69 — and who went on to found the colony of Pennsylvania. He is remembered chiefly as a colonist and advocate of religious toleration, but his most durable piece of writing is a small, unshowy book of aphorisms: Some Fruits of Solitude (licensed 1693) and its sequel More Fruits of Solitude (1718). Edmund Gosse, introducing a 1903 reprint, argued the maxims came out of the years when Penn was out of favour and in hiding after the fall of James II — the enforced leisure Penn thanks God for in the book itself.

misattribution.heading: Right author, reshaped quote
misattribution.intro: Nobody is stealing this one from William Penn — he wrote every word. What has drifted is the shape of it: which book it comes from, how many sentences it is, and what kind of writing it was in the first place.

items.why: Penn numbered them separately: “127. They that love beyond the World, cannot be separated by it.” and “128. Death cannot kill, what never dies.” The familiar single-sentence quotation runs two distinct maxims together, as the 1718 first edition ↗ shows.

The lines are in the second part, More Fruits of Solitude. Because the two parts are usually bound together, quote sites credit a merged title — Goodreads files the passage under ‘Some Fruits of Solitude/ More Fruits of Solitude’ ↗.
Funeral-reading sites give the passage a title and break it into lines, as on this collection of funeral poems ↗. Penn wrote numbered prose aphorisms; the stanzas are a modern layout.

Rowling’s epigraph draws on the same “Union of Friends” heading but on later maxims — 131 to 134, beginning “Death is but crossing the world” — as HogwartsProfessor documents ↗. These two lines are not the epigraph.

misattribution.truthLine: Penn wrote both sentences, in this order, as maxims 127 and 128 of the “Union of Friends” section of More Fruits of Solitude, printed in London in 1718 — readable in the first edition ↗.

context.heading: A book written in enforced retirement
lead: Penn is remembered for a colony, not a commonplace book — but the Fruits of Solitude maxims are the part of him that still gets read aloud. Edmund Gosse, introducing the 1903 reprint, placed their writing in the stretch after the fall of James II when Penn, suspected of corresponding with the exiled king, had a warrant out against him and spent months in hiding; he was not fully reinstated until he appeared before William III in Council in the autumn of 1693. The book’s own author, Gosse noted, blesses God for his retirement and says he never had so much leisure in his life before.

The “Union of Friends” heading gathers eight short maxims on the same idea: that friendship survives distance, and that distance is all death is. More Fruits of Solitude was printed in London in 1718, the year Penn died. Read in that order, the famous line is the opening move of an argument rather than an epitaph — though an epitaph is almost entirely what it has become.
context.detailsSummary: The section that became a Harry Potter epigraph
detailsBody: J. K. Rowling opened Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows with a passage from this same “Union of Friends” section — but not with these lines. The epigraph runs from “Death is but crossing the world, as friends do the seas” to “because immortal,” which is maxims 131 to 134, as HogwartsProfessor sets out line by line ↗. It is half of the eight aphorisms Penn filed under that heading.

The other half — maxims 127 and 128 — had a separate afterlife in funeral orders of service, where they are routinely set as verse under a title, as on this British funeral-readings site ↗. Penn wrote prose.

sourcesVerified.claim: The scanned 1718 London edition of More Fruits of Solitude contains, under the heading "Union of Friends", maxim 127 "They that love beyond the World, cannot be separated by it." and maxim 128 "Death cannot kill, what never dies.", continuing through maxim 134; the title page reads "Printed and Sold by the Assigns of J. Sowle, at the Bible in George-Yard, Lombard-Street".
Internet Archive item record: "More fruits of solitude: being the second part of reflections and maxims, relating to the conduct of human life", William Penn, dated 1718, a scanned copy of 122 pages.

The 1903 H. M. Caldwell reprint reproduces the "UNION of FRIENDS" maxims 127-134 within the section headed "More Fruits of Solitude, BEING The Second Part of Reflections and Maxims"; Edmund Gosse's introduction states the first edition was licensed 24 May 1693 and was anonymous, that "More Fruits of Solitude" made its earliest appearance in 1718, that the reprint gives the text of 1718 rather than 1693, and that Penn was born on 14 October 1644 and was in hiding after the fall of James II until appearing before William III in Council in autumn 1693.
Internet Archive item record: "Some Fruits of Solitude: By William Penn", publisher H. M. Caldwell co, 1903, 269 pages, digitised by Google from the New York Public Library, marked NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT.

Wikiquote's sourced William Penn page carries the passage beginning "They that love beyond the world cannot be separated by it. Death cannot kill, what never dies" through "because Immortal", in its Part II subsection, cited to numbers 127-134.

HogwartsProfessor states that J. K. Rowling's epigraph to Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows is drawn from the "Union of Friends" section of Penn's More Fruits of Solitude, specifically sentences 131-134, which is half of the eight aphorisms under that heading.
This funeral-readings site presents the passage as a funeral poem titled "They That Love Beyond the World", credited to William Penn, filed under its Poems for Funerals section.
Goodreads credits the passage to "William Penn, Some Fruits of Solitude/ More Fruits of Solitude" - a merged title conflating the two parts.
